nonTeachingWeeks.what: Routines, math tools, and the beginning-of-year screening (counting to 100, facts within 5, numeral writing).
End of the first quarter: report-card checks and family conferences.
The short week before winter break: fact games and review, no new lesson.
Middle-of-year benchmark window.
End of the third quarter: report-card checks and spring conferences.
End-of-year benchmark window.
Last week of school: review stations and summer practice packets.

units.title: Addition and Subtraction Within 10
units.why: The year starts where Kindergarten ended, and every later unit leans on the facts and the equal sign taught here.

lessons.title: True or false?
lessons.objective: Children decide whether an equation within 10 is true or false, including equations with the total first (8 = 5 + 3) and with a sum or difference on both sides (9 - 2 = 3 + 4).
lessons.page: Level 1: twelve equations within 10, each with a "true" box and a "false" box to tick: four of the usual kind (5 + 3 = 8), four with the total first (8 = 5 + 3, 7 = 7), four with a sum or a difference on both sides (9 - 2 = 3 + 4). Five of the twelve are false. Level 2: the child makes each false equation true by changing one number, then writes two true equations of their own with the total first.

units.title: Adding and Subtracting Within 20
units.why: Once the facts within 10 are firm, the class learns the strategies that carry them across ten: doubles, near doubles, making ten, and thinking addition.

lessons.title: Near doubles
lessons.objective: Children solve sums such as 6 + 7 as a double and one more (6 + 6 + 1), with sums up to 19.
lessons.page: Top half: six pairs of ten-frame pictures, a double and its neighbor side by side (6 + 6 and 6 + 7); the child writes both sums. Bottom half: ten near doubles from 3 + 4 to 9 + 10 with the frame 6 + 7 = 6 + 6 + _ = _. Sums up to 19.

lessons.title: Make ten to add
lessons.objective: Children add 9, 8 or 7 and a number from 4 to 9 by filling a ten-frame first, and write the steps, such as 8 + 5 = 10 + 3 = 13.
lessons.page: Level 1: eight tasks, each with two ten-frames; the first shows 9, 8 or 7 counters, the second 4 to 9 counters in another color. The child crosses out the counters that move, draws them in the first frame, and completes 8 + 5 = 10 + _ = _. Level 2: the same sums with empty frames to draw in. Level 3: equations only (9 + 6 = 10 + _ = _). Sums from 11 to 18; the two numbers never make exactly 10.

lessons.title: Think addition to subtract
lessons.objective: Children solve subtractions from 11 to 18 by finding the missing addend, such as 13 - 8 by asking 8 + ? = 13.
lessons.page: Ten tasks. Each shows a subtraction (13 - 8 = _), a number bond with the whole and one part filled in, and the helper equation 8 + _ = 13. The child fills the bond, the helper equation, and then the subtraction. Wholes from 11 to 18; the part taken away is 5 to 9.

units.title: Story Problems Within 20
units.why: With strategies to 20 in hand, the class can give its attention to what a story asks; the hard story types need their own weeks before winter.

lessons.title: Find the missing part
lessons.objective: Children solve put-together stories within 20 in which the total and one part are known, with a bar model and an equation with a box for the missing part.
lessons.page: Six stories within 20 ("12 children are on the playground. 7 are girls. How many are boys?"). Each has a bar model, one long bar for the total above two parts, in which the child writes the two known numbers and a question mark; an equation frame with a box (7 + _ = 12); and an answer line with a label. Four stories ask for a part and two for the total.

lessons.title: What happened in the middle?
lessons.objective: Children solve stories within 20 in which the start and the end are known and the change is missing (some came or some left), and write equations such as 8 + ? = 13 and 12 - ? = 7.
lessons.page: Six stories ('8 children are on the bus. Some more get on. Now there are 13. How many got on?'). Each has a strip of three boxes for start, change and end with a plus or minus sign to circle, space for a drawing, and an equation frame with the box in the middle (8 + _ = 13). Level 1: within 10; level 2: within 20, three stories of each kind. The child fills the strip, draws, and writes the equation and the answer with its label.

lessons.title: How many more? How many fewer?
lessons.objective: Children compare two amounts within 20 in a story, show them as two bars, and find how many more or how many fewer with an addition or a subtraction equation.
lessons.page: Six stories ('Mia has 12 stickers. Ben has 7 stickers. How many more stickers does Mia have?'). Each has two rows of 20 empty squares, one under the other, with the names in front; the child colors each amount from the left, rings the squares that stick out, and writes an equation (7 + _ = 12 or 12 - 7 = _) and the answer. Level 1 asks 'how many more'; level 2 mixes 'more' and 'fewer'. Amounts from 3 to 20.

lessons.title: Stories with three numbers
lessons.objective: Children solve story problems that add three numbers with a total up to 20, with a drawing and an equation, and look for two numbers that make ten first.
lessons.page: Six stories with three groups ('4 red, 6 blue and 5 green marbles. How many marbles?'). Each has a drawing box and the frame _ + _ + _ = _. The child draws the three groups, rings two numbers that make ten or a double when there are some, and writes the equation and the answer. Each number is 1 to 9; totals from 8 to 20.

units.title: Tens and Ones
units.why: Place value opens the second half of the year; teens and whole tens come first, then any two-digit number.

lessons.title: Teen numbers: one ten and some ones
lessons.objective: Children build the numbers 11 to 19 with one ten-rod and loose cubes and write them as one ten and some ones.
lessons.page: Top half: eight pictures of one ten-rod and 1 to 9 loose cubes; the child writes '1 ten _ ones' and the number. Bottom half: six written numbers from 11 to 19; the child draws one rod and the right number of cubes for each.

lessons.title: Count the tens: 10 to 90
lessons.objective: Children count 1 to 9 ten-rods, say how many tens there are with no ones left over, and write the number from 10 to 90.
lessons.page: Top half: eight pictures of 1 to 9 ten-rods and no loose cubes; the child writes '_ tens 0 ones' and the number. Bottom half: six numbers from 10 to 90; the child draws that many rods and writes how many tens.

units.title: The Hundreds Chart and Skip Counting
units.why: The chart turns tens and ones into a map; 10 more and 10 less on it prepare the adding of tens in the next unit.

units.title: Adding Within 100 and Subtracting Tens
units.why: This is the hardest number work of Grade 1 and needs tens and ones and the hundreds chart behind it, so it comes in early spring.

lessons.title: Add tens to a number
lessons.objective: Children add a multiple of ten to a two-digit number in their heads (34 + 20) and say that only the tens digit changes, with sums up to 99.
lessons.page: Level 1: ten equations of a two-digit number plus 10, 20, 30, 40, 50 or 60 (34 + 20 = _), with a small hundreds chart at the top for jumping down the rows. Level 2: ten equations with no chart, four of them with a missing number (34 + _ = 64). Sums up to 99; the ones digit never changes.

lessons.title: Subtract tens from tens
lessons.objective: Children subtract a multiple of ten from a multiple of ten from 10 to 90 (70 - 30) by taking away ten-rods, and say why 7 tens take away 3 tens leaves 4 tens.
lessons.page: Level 1: eight pictures of 2 to 9 ten-rods with a subtraction (70 - 30 = _); the child crosses out the rods taken away and completes '7 tens - 3 tens = _ tens' and the equation. Level 2: ten equations with no picture, two of them with a missing number (60 - _ = 20). All numbers are whole tens from 10 to 90; the answer is at least 10.

lessons.title: Add ones to a two-digit number
lessons.objective: Children add a one-digit number to a two-digit number when the ones stay under ten (32 + 5), and say that the tens do not change.
lessons.page: Level 1: eight tasks; each shows a two-digit number drawn as rods and cubes and a sum (32 + 5 = _). The child draws the cubes that are added in another color and writes the sum. Level 2: ten equations with a place-value frame (tens and ones boxes) and no picture. The ones add up to 9 at most; sums up to 99.

lessons.title: Add ones and make a new ten
lessons.objective: Children add a one-digit number to a two-digit number when the ones make a new ten (27 + 5), trade ten cubes for a rod, and write the steps, such as 27 + 5 = 30 + 2 = 32.
lessons.page: Level 1: six tasks; each shows the two-digit number as rods and cubes and the added ones as cubes in another color. The child rings ten cubes, draws the new rod, and writes the sum. Level 2: eight tasks with the frame 27 + 5 = 30 + _ = _ (first to the next ten, then the rest). Level 3: equations only. The ones always add up to 10 or more; sums up to 99.

lessons.title: Add two two-digit numbers: tens with tens, ones with ones
lessons.objective: Children add two two-digit numbers with no new ten (34 + 25) by adding the tens and the ones apart with rods and cubes, and write the sum up to 99.
lessons.page: Level 1: six tasks; both numbers are drawn as rods and cubes, and the child counts all the rods, then all the cubes, and completes '_ tens and _ ones = _'. Level 2: eight tasks with the frame 34 + 25 = (30 + 20) + (4 + 5) = _ and space for a quick drawing of sticks and dots. The ones add up to 9 at most; sums up to 99.

lessons.title: Add two two-digit numbers and make a new ten
lessons.objective: Children add two two-digit numbers when the ones make a new ten (36 + 28), with a drawing of rods and cubes, and tell a partner why the new ten joins the tens.
lessons.page: Six tasks. Each has the sum (36 + 28 = _), a tens-and-ones mat to draw both numbers as sticks and dots, and the sentence '_ tens and _ ones = _'. The child draws both numbers, rings ten dots and draws one stick for them, then counts sticks and dots. The last task asks: 'Tell your partner why you drew a new stick.' The ones add up to 10 to 17; sums up to 99.

units.title: Time and Coins
units.why: Clocks and coins use counting by fives and tens from the chart unit and fit the spring weeks around the benchmark.

lessons.title: Match the clocks
lessons.objective: Children read times to the hour and the half hour on clocks with hands and on digital clocks, match the two, and write the time in digits (7:00, 7:30).
lessons.page: Top half: six clocks with hands (three on the hour, three at half past) and six digital clocks in mixed order; the child draws a line from each clock with hands to the digital clock that shows the same time. Bottom half: six clocks with hands, each with an empty digital display in which the child writes the time (4:30), and two digital times for which the child circles the right clock of two (for 2:30, the hour hand halfway between 2 and 3 or pointing straight at 2).

units.title: Measuring, Graphs, and Shapes
units.why: Measuring, graphing and shapes close the year with real things in hand, and halves and fourths of shapes follow the half hour on the clock.

lessons.title: No gaps, no overlaps
lessons.objective: Children measure real objects by laying paper clips or cubes end to end from one end to the other with no gaps and no overlaps, and find the mistake in a row of units that was laid wrong.
lessons.page: Top half: six pictures of an object with a row of units under it; in three the units are laid right, and in three there is a gap, an overlap, or a row that starts or ends in the wrong place. The child ticks right or wrong and circles the mistake. Bottom half: four objects with empty space under them and a strip of same-size squares to cut out and glue; the child lays the squares end to end and writes "about _ squares long". Lengths from 3 to 9 units.

lessons.title: Halves and fourths
lessons.objective: Children fold and cut paper circles and rectangles into two and four equal shares, name the shares as halves and fourths (quarters), and say that four fourths make the whole.
lessons.page: Level 1: twelve circles and rectangles cut into 2 or 4 parts, some equal and some not; the child colors only the shapes with equal shares and writes 'halves' or 'fourths' under them. Level 2: eight whole circles and rectangles; the child draws lines to split each into halves or fourths as asked and colors one share. Level 3: four sentences to finish ('The pizza has _ fourths. One half is _ than one fourth.'). The two live screen activities on equal shares are the screen task.

leftOut.what: Odd and even numbers
leftOut.why: Odd and even is a Grade 2 standard (2.OA.C.3) and Grade 2 has its own lesson; the three days go to the strategies within 20.

leftOut.what: Yesterday, today, tomorrow, and the months
leftOut.why: The calendar is taught every morning in the calendar routine with Calendar Wall, not in the math block.

leftOut.what: Ordinal numbers to tenth
leftOut.why: Ordinal numbers are no Grade 1 standard, and Kindergarten already has a lesson on them; the three days go to story problems.

leftOut.what: Patterns: two are missing
leftOut.why: Repeating patterns are no Grade 1 standard; the lesson stays on the site as extra practice outside the year plan.

leftOut.what: 1.OA.A.1: start-unknown stories and compare stories with the bigger or smaller amount unknown
leftOut.why: No days are left; the class most needs the missing part, the missing change and 'how many more', and the other types open Grade 2.

leftOut.what: 1.OA.C.6: subtracting through ten (13 - 4 = 13 - 3 - 1) and a fluency lesson within 20
leftOut.why: Think addition is the one subtraction strategy every child needs; fluency within 20 is a daily routine and a Grade 2 goal.

leftOut.what: 1.OA.D.8: a third lesson with the unknown at the start
leftOut.why: The missing-change stories and the lesson Find the missing number cover the unknown in the middle; the start is Grade 2 work for most children.

leftOut.what: 1.NBT.A.1: counting past 100 to 120
leftOut.why: Counting to 120 belongs to the daily count on the chart; there are no days left for a lesson.

leftOut.what: 1.NBT.B.3: a lesson on the signs <, > and =
leftOut.why: The lesson Compare and order two-digit numbers stays the one lesson; the signs are added to its second day.

leftOut.what: 1.NBT.C.4: a sixth lesson (explaining why the way works)
leftOut.why: Explaining is asked on the last task of each of the five lessons instead of in a lesson of its own.

leftOut.what: 1.MD.A.2: a third lesson on laying units
leftOut.why: The three-day lesson Measure length with squares and the new lesson No gaps, no overlaps hold the hands-on work; no days are left.

leftOut.what: point 1:days-months-seasons
leftOut.why: The calendar belongs to the morning routine with Calendar Wall, not to the math block.

nonTeachingWeeks.what: Routines, math tools, and the beginning-of-year screening (facts within 20, place value to 100).
End of the first quarter: report-card checks, the first facts check, and family conferences.
The short week before winter break: fact games and review, no new lesson.
Middle-of-year benchmark window and the second facts check.
End of the third quarter: report-card checks, the third facts check, and spring conferences.
End-of-year benchmark window and the last facts check.
Last week of school: review stations and summer practice packets.

units.title: Fact Strategies Within 20
units.why: The year opens with the four strategies behind the facts within 20, so the five-minute daily fact strip can run in every later unit.

lessons.title: Make ten to add
lessons.objective: Children add two one-digit numbers with a sum from 11 to 18 by splitting one of them to make ten, such as 8 + 6 = 8 + 2 + 4 = 14.
lessons.page: Twelve sums from 11 to 18 with one addend 7, 8 or 9. Under the second addend is a small split with two empty circles; the child writes the two parts (the part that makes ten first) and completes 8 + 6 = 10 + _ = _. The first four tasks show two ten-frames as a help; the last four are the turned-around sums (6 + 8).

lessons.title: Doubles and near doubles
lessons.objective: Children say the doubles from 6 + 6 to 9 + 9 from memory and use them to solve near doubles, such as 7 + 8 = 7 + 7 + 1.
lessons.page: Top third: the doubles from 5 + 5 to 9 + 9 to write from memory. Middle: eight near doubles (6 + 7, 7 + 8, 8 + 9 and their turn-arounds), each with the frame 7 + 8 = 7 + 7 + _ = _. Bottom: six subtractions that are halves of doubles (16 - 8, 14 - 7) and near them (15 - 7).

lessons.title: Use ten to subtract
lessons.objective: Children subtract a one-digit number from a number from 11 to 18 by going back to ten first, such as 15 - 7 = 15 - 5 - 2 = 8.
lessons.page: Twelve subtractions from 11 to 18 in which a ten is crossed. Under the number taken away is a small split with two empty circles; the child writes the part that gets back to 10 first, then the rest, and completes 15 - 7 = 10 - _ = _. The first four tasks show a full ten-frame and a second frame with the ones to cross out; the last four have no split printed.

lessons.title: Think addition to subtract, and start the daily facts
lessons.objective: Children solve subtraction facts within 20 by thinking of the addition fact (15 - 9 as 9 + ? = 15), and begin the five-minute daily fact strip they keep all year.
lessons.page: Page 1: eight fact triangles (whole from 11 to 18 at the top, two parts below, one part missing); the child fills the triangle and writes the two additions and two subtractions of the family. Page 2: the first week of daily fact strips, five strips of ten mixed facts within 20, each with a box for 'how many I knew right away' and a small chart to color. A new sheet of strips goes with every later unit.

units.title: Place Value to 1,000
units.why: Hundreds, tens and ones must be firm before any adding within 100 and 1,000, so place value takes the early fall.

lessons.title: Ten tens make one hundred
lessons.objective: Children bundle ten ten-rods into one hundred, count hundreds, tens and ones in a picture, and write the number up to 1,000.
lessons.page: Top half: six pictures of 10 to 19 ten-rods; the child rings ten rods, writes '1 hundred _ tens' and the number (130). Bottom half: six pictures of 1 to 9 hundred-flats alone; the child counts by hundreds and writes '_ hundreds 0 tens 0 ones' and the number (100 to 900).

lessons.title: Numbers with a zero
lessons.objective: Children read and write three-digit numbers that have a zero in the tens or the ones place (406, 460) as numerals, in words and in expanded form.
lessons.page: A table of ten rows with four columns: blocks, numeral, expanded form, number name. In each row one or two columns are filled and the child fills the rest (blocks are drawn as squares, sticks and dots). Every number from 101 to 990 has a zero in the tens or the ones place; the pairs 406 and 460, 307 and 370 stand one under the other. Last task: circle the right numeral of three for 'five hundred eight' (58, 508, 580).

units.title: Adding and Subtracting Within 100
units.why: This is the heart of Grade 2: it follows place value directly and gets the longest stretch of the fall, from number line and chart to written columns.

lessons.title: Jumps on an empty number line
lessons.objective: Children add and subtract two-digit numbers within 100 on an empty number line: jumps of ten first, then the ones, or a jump to the next ten and then the rest.
lessons.page: Level 1: six tasks with no ten crossed (34 + 25, 67 - 30), each with an empty line on which the start number is marked; the child draws jumps of ten, then jumps for the ones, and writes every landing number. Level 2: eight tasks that cross a ten (47 + 28, 62 - 37); the child jumps the tens, then to the next ten, then the rest. Level 3: four tasks with a bare line and nothing marked. All numbers within 100.

lessons.title: Add tens and ones, then put them together
lessons.objective: Children add two two-digit numbers with a sum up to 100 when the ones make a new ten (47 + 38), with a drawing of sticks and dots and the partial sums 70 + 15.
lessons.page: Eight tasks. Each has the sum (47 + 38 = _), a tens-and-ones mat for a drawing of sticks and dots, and the frame 40 + 30 = _, 7 + 8 = _, _ + _ = _. The child draws, rings ten dots for a new stick, and fills the three lines. The ones add up to 10 to 18 in six tasks and stay under 10 in two; sums from 41 to 100.

lessons.title: Subtract and open a ten
lessons.objective: Children subtract a two-digit number from a two-digit number within 100 when there are not enough ones (52 - 27), by opening one ten into ten ones in a drawing.
lessons.page: Eight tasks. Each has the difference (52 - 27 = _) and a tens-and-ones mat on which the first number is already drawn as sticks and dots. The child first answers 'Enough ones? yes / no', crosses out one stick and draws ten dots when the answer is no, then crosses out what is taken away and writes what is left. Six tasks need a ten opened and two do not.

lessons.title: Add three and four two-digit numbers
lessons.objective: Children add three or four two-digit numbers with a sum up to 100 in columns and look for ones that make ten first.
lessons.page: Top half: four sums of three two-digit numbers and four sums of four two-digit numbers written in columns with a tens and a ones column and a small box for the new tens; the child rings ones that make ten before adding. Bottom half: two short stories with three or four amounts (points in four rounds of a game). Each number is 10 to 39; sums from 40 to 100.

lessons.title: Why does it work?
lessons.objective: Children explain with blocks or a drawing why a way of adding or subtracting within 100 works, and compare two worked ways for the same sum, such as 38 + 25.
lessons.page: Number talk: the teacher shows one sum (38 + 25, later 63 - 28) and two worked ways side by side (tens and ones apart; a jump to the next ten). Pairs say what each child did and why both give the same answer, then show it with blocks. Listen for place-value words ('3 tens and 2 tens', 'I made a new ten from 8 ones and 2 ones') and not only 'I carried the 1'.

units.title: Story Problems Within 100
units.why: Stories come right after the class can add and subtract within 100, so the numbers no longer stand in the way of the thinking.

lessons.title: One-step stories with a bar model
lessons.objective: Children solve one-step story problems within 100 in which the end or the change is missing, with a bar model and an equation with a box for the unknown.
lessons.page: Six stories with two-digit numbers: three with the end missing and three with the change missing ("34 children were on the playground. Some more came. Now there are 52."). Each has an empty bar model (one long bar over two parts) to label, an equation frame with a box (34 + _ = 52), and an answer line with a label.

lessons.title: What was there at the start?
lessons.objective: Children solve one-step story problems within 100 in which the start is missing ("Sam had some cards. He gave away 25 and has 38 left."), with a bar model and an equation that begins with a box.
lessons.page: Six stories with two-digit numbers and the start missing: three in which something is added ("Some birds sat in the tree. 17 more came. Now there are 45.") and three in which something is taken away. Each has an empty bar model to label, an equation frame that begins with the box (_ + 17 = 45, _ - 25 = 38), a second line for the equation the child uses to solve it (45 - 17 = _), and an answer line with a label.

lessons.title: Compare stories: more and fewer
lessons.objective: Children solve compare stories within 100, including stories in which the larger or the smaller amount is missing ('Ana has 15 fewer than Ben'), with two bars and an equation.
lessons.page: Six stories with two-digit numbers: two ask for the difference, two for the larger amount, two for the smaller amount; in two of them the word 'fewer' points to an addition. Each has two empty bars one under the other with name tags and a bracket for the difference; the child labels the bars, writes an equation with a box, and answers with a label.

lessons.title: Two-step stories
lessons.objective: Children solve story problems within 100 that need two steps of adding or subtracting, and write an equation for each step.
lessons.page: Five stories with two-digit numbers ("There were 34 birds in the tree. 12 flew away, then 25 more came. How many birds now?"). Each has two equation lines marked Step 1 and Step 2 and an answer line with a label. In the first two stories a helper question for step 1 is printed; in the last three it is not. Both steps add or subtract within 100.

units.title: Adding and Subtracting Within 1,000
units.why: The same moves go on to three-digit numbers after winter break, with blocks first and written ways after them.

lessons.title: Add three-digit numbers and make a new ten or hundred
lessons.objective: Children add two three-digit numbers with a sum up to 1,000 when the ones make a new ten, the tens make a new hundred, or both (268 + 157), with a place-value drawing and a written way.
lessons.page: Eight tasks. Each has the sum in columns with boxes for the new ten and the new hundred, and beside it a hundreds-tens-ones mat for a drawing of squares, sticks and dots. Three tasks make a new ten, two a new hundred, three both. The child draws, rings ten of a kind, and writes the sum. Sums from 300 to 1,000.

lessons.title: Subtract three-digit numbers and open a ten or a hundred
lessons.objective: Children subtract within 1,000 when a ten, a hundred, or both must be opened (432 - 157), with a place-value drawing and a written way.
lessons.page: Eight tasks. Each has the difference in columns and a hundreds-tens-ones mat on which the first number is drawn. The child answers 'Enough ones? Enough tens?', opens a stick or a square when needed, crosses out, and writes the difference. Three tasks open a ten, two a hundred, three both. No digit of the first number is zero.

lessons.title: Subtract across a zero
lessons.objective: Children subtract from three-digit numbers with a zero in the tens place or from whole hundreds (304 - 128, 500 - 236), opening a hundred first and then a ten.
lessons.page: Eight tasks in columns with a hundreds-tens-ones mat: four from numbers with a zero in the tens place (304, 507), four from whole hundreds (500, 800). The first two are worked halfway (the hundred already opened into ten tens). On each task the child checks by adding the answer and the number taken away on a line below.

units.title: Time, Money, and Measuring Length
units.why: Clocks and coins count by fives and tens and use the adding within 100; length comes last in the unit, so the line plot of measured lengths follows directly.

lessons.title: Count mixed coins
lessons.objective: Children name pennies, nickels, dimes and quarters, sort a handful from the largest value to the smallest, and count on to find the total up to 100 cents with the cent sign.
lessons.page: The same page as Counting Coins with larger amounts: groups of four to eight mixed coins with quarters, totals from 26 cents to 100 cents. The child writes the running count under each coin (25, 35, 40, 41) and the total with the cent sign. The top level asks which coins make a given amount in two different ways.

lessons.title: Same length, two units
lessons.objective: Children measure the same object in inches and in centimeters (and in feet and inches), and say why the smaller unit gives the larger number.
lessons.page: A recording page for real things: six rows (pencil, book, desk edge, shoe, glue stick, crayon), each with two boxes, 'about _ inches' and 'about _ centimeters'. Below: three sentences to finish ('I needed more _ than _ because a centimeter is _ than an inch.') and two picture tasks in which one ribbon is measured with a row of long units and a row of short units to count. The child measures the real things with a class ruler, never the pictures.

lessons.title: Estimate, then measure
lessons.objective: Children estimate lengths in inches, feet, centimeters and meters with body benchmarks (a fingertip, a thumb joint, a ruler, the width of the door), then measure and compare.
lessons.page: Hands-on routine: the class learns four benchmarks, then pairs estimate the desk, the door, the rug and a pencil before they measure them; the page is only the recording sheet with three columns (my estimate, my measure, how far off). Listen for estimates that name a unit and lean on a benchmark ('about 3 rulers, so 3 feet'), and for children who change the next estimate after a measure.

lessons.title: Length story problems
lessons.objective: Children solve story problems within 100 about lengths in the same unit (inches, feet, centimeters or meters), with a drawing of the lengths and an equation with a box for the unknown.
lessons.page: Six stories about lengths ('A ribbon is 45 cm long. Lea cuts off 18 cm. How long is it now?'; 'The red rope is 36 feet, the blue rope is 27 feet longer.'). Each has space to draw the lengths as bars or on a number line, an equation frame with a box, and an answer line with the unit. Two put lengths together, two take a length away, two compare. All numbers within 100, one unit per story.

units.title: Bar Graphs, Picture Graphs, and Line Plots
units.why: Data follows measuring, because the line plot needs lengths the children measured themselves; bar and picture graphs come first as the easier graphs.

lessons.title: Make a picture graph
lessons.objective: Children draw a picture graph with one picture for each thing for four groups of 1 to 10, and answer how many more, how many fewer and how many in all from it.
lessons.page: Top: a small table of counts for four groups (the favorite fruit of a class: apple 7, banana 4, grapes 9, orange 5). Middle: an empty picture graph with four rows of ten boxes and the key "one face = 1 child"; the child writes the title and the group names and draws one face in a box for each child. Bottom: five questions ("How many more children chose grapes than bananas? How many chose apple or orange in all?"), each with an equation line. A second version has the graph standing in columns.

lessons.title: Measure and make a line plot
lessons.objective: Children measure ten real objects to the nearest inch or centimeter with a ruler, write the lengths in a table, and show them as Xs on a line plot.
lessons.page: A recording page: a table with ten rows (object, length) for ten real things of one kind (ten pencils from the class, ten shoes), an empty number line with twelve tick marks whose numbers the child writes after finding the shortest and the longest, and space for the Xs above it. Three questions follow ('Which length did we find most often? How many are longer than _?'). Nothing printed on the page is to be measured.

units.title: Equal Groups, Shapes, and Equal Shares
units.why: Arrays, shapes and equal shares close the year as one unit, from rows and columns to rectangles of squares to shapes cut into halves, thirds and fourths: the bridge to multiplication and fractions in Grade 3.

lessons.title: Rows and columns of squares
lessons.objective: Children split a rectangle into rows and columns of same-size squares (up to 5 by 5) and count the squares by rows.
lessons.page: Top half: four rectangles with tick marks on two sides; the child draws the lines with a ruler to make rows and columns and completes '_ rows, _ columns, _ squares' and an addition of equal rows (4 + 4 + 4 = 12). Bottom half: four rectangles with one row and one column of squares already drawn; the child finishes the grid and counts. Up to 5 rows and 5 columns. In class children first cover a paper rectangle with square tiles.

leftOut.what: Read a calendar
leftOut.why: The calendar is read every morning in the calendar routine with Calendar Wall, not in the math block.

leftOut.what: Each picture counts as two
leftOut.why: Picture graphs with a scale are a Grade 3 standard (3.MD.B.3), and Grade 3 has the lesson.

leftOut.what: Find a square on a grid
leftOut.why: Grid coordinates are no Grade 2 standard; the days go to the line plot the children measure themselves.

leftOut.what: Count by threes and fours
leftOut.why: Grade 2 counts by fives, tens and hundreds; threes and fours belong to the multiplication facts of Grade 3.

leftOut.what: Share fairly and make groups
leftOut.why: Division is a Grade 3 standard, and Grade 3 has a lesson with the same tool.

leftOut.what: A fraction of a group
leftOut.why: Grade 2 fractions are equal shares of one shape; a fraction of a set is beyond the grade.

leftOut.what: Is it a line of symmetry?
leftOut.why: Line symmetry is a Grade 4 standard; the three days go to adding and subtracting within 100.

leftOut.what: Finish the other half
leftOut.why: Line symmetry is a Grade 4 standard; the three days go to adding and subtracting within 1,000.

leftOut.what: Which one matches the shadow?
leftOut.why: A puzzle lesson with no Grade 2 standard; it stays on the site as extra practice outside the year plan.

leftOut.what: 2.OA.B.2: two more strategy lessons and more fluency lessons
leftOut.why: Four strategy lessons launch the facts; after that fluency is the daily five-minute strip and four facts checks, not more lessons.

leftOut.what: 2.OA.A.1: four more story lessons (one for each story type)
leftOut.why: The four lessons hold every type; the length stories and money stories add more story work in spring.

leftOut.what: 2.NBT.A.1.b: a separate lesson on 100 to 900 as a count of hundreds
leftOut.why: It is the second half of the page of Ten tens make one hundred; a whole lesson would be thin.

leftOut.what: 2.NBT.A.2: two more lessons on counting within 1,000
leftOut.why: No days are left; counting across hundreds is practiced with Choral Counting in Count by fives and tens and in the daily count.

leftOut.what: 2.NBT.B.5: checking with the other operation, partners of 100, and mental math as lessons of their own
leftOut.why: No days are left; the check by adding is built into the page of Subtract across a zero.

leftOut.what: 2.NBT.B.7: three more lessons, and 2.NBT.B.8: ten more and ten less across a hundred
leftOut.why: The five lessons within 1,000 cover no regrouping, one regrouping, two, and the zero; 295 + 10 is practiced in the daily count.

leftOut.what: 2.MD.A.1: a second lesson on choosing the unit and the tool
leftOut.why: Choosing a unit is part of Estimate, then measure.

leftOut.what: 2.MD.C.7: three more time lessons (the hour hand between numbers, quarter past and quarter to, a.m. and p.m.)
leftOut.why: No days are left; the three-day lesson and its Quarter Hours page keep quarter hours, and a.m. and p.m. are named there on day 3.

leftOut.what: 2.MD.C.8: lessons on like coins and on dollar bills
leftOut.why: Like coins are the first level of Count mixed coins, and the shopping lesson writes prices with the dollar sign.

leftOut.what: point 2:flat-or-solid
leftOut.why: Its standard is K.G.A.3, so the point is used in Kindergarten.

nonTeachingWeeks.what: Routines, math tools, and the beginning-of-year screening (facts within 20, adding and subtracting within 100).
End of the first quarter: report-card checks and family conferences.
The short week before winter break: fact games and review, no new lesson.
Middle-of-year benchmark window and the multiplication facts check.
End of the third quarter: report-card checks and spring conferences.
Review week before the state test: mixed practice from all units and test format.
State test window.
Last week of school: review stations and summer practice packets.

units.title: Rounding, Adding, and Subtracting Within 1,000
units.why: The year opens with numbers the class knows from Grade 2, and rounding is needed later to check story problems.

units.title: Starting Multiplication
units.why: Multiplication starts in the fall, because the facts need the rest of the year of daily practice.

units.title: Division and the Facts to 100
units.why: Division follows multiplication at once, so each fact is learned with its family; the same unit then breaks the hard facts apart and starts the daily fact routine that runs to the end of the year.

lessons.title: Break a hard fact into two easy ones
lessons.objective: Children split an array for a fact with 6, 7, 8 or 9 into two arrays they know and add the two products, such as 7 x 8 = 5 x 8 + 2 x 8 = 40 + 16.
lessons.page: Level 1: six dot arrays (6 x 7, 7 x 8, 6 x 9 and others) with a dashed line already drawn after the fifth row; the child completes 7 x 8 = 5 x 8 + 2 x 8 = _ + _ = _. Level 2: six arrays with no line; the child draws the line where it helps and writes the three steps. Level 3: eight facts with no array and the frame 8 x 6 = (5 x 6) + (_ x 6) = _. One factor is always 6, 7, 8 or 9; products up to 81.

lessons.title: The facts we still need
lessons.objective: Children mark on a multiplication chart to 10 x 10 the facts they already own (times 1, 2, 5 and 10 and their turn-arounds), list the facts left to learn, and start the daily fact practice with the matching division facts.
lessons.page: Page 1: an empty multiplication chart from 1 x 1 to 10 x 10; the child fills and colors the rows and columns for 1, 2, 5 and 10, then circles the boxes still white and writes each of those facts once with its product. Page 2: the first week of daily fact strips, five strips of ten facts, each multiplication next to its division (6 x 4 = _, 24 / 4 = _), with a box for 'how many I knew right away'. A new sheet of strips goes with every later unit.

lessons.title: Multiply by tens
lessons.objective: Children multiply a one-digit number by a multiple of ten from 10 to 90 (4 x 60) by thinking of tens: 4 x 6 tens = 24 tens = 240.
lessons.page: Top half: six tasks with a picture of ten-rods in equal groups (4 groups of 6 rods); the child completes 4 x 6 tens = _ tens = _. Bottom half: twelve equations in pairs, the fact and its tens partner (3 x 7 = _, 3 x 70 = _), and two short stories (5 boxes of 40 pencils). One factor is 2 to 9, the other a whole ten from 10 to 90.

units.title: Story Problems with All Four Operations
units.why: Two-step problems need all four operations and rounding, so they come when the facts are in daily practice and stay before the spring test.

lessons.title: Two-step stories: add and subtract
lessons.objective: Children solve two-step story problems with adding and subtracting within 1,000, with a bar model for each step.
lessons.page: Five stories with three-digit numbers ('The school had 345 books. It bought 128 more and gave 96 away. How many books now?'). Each has two empty bar models marked Step 1 and Step 2, an equation line for each step, and an answer line with a label. The first two stories give the helper question for step 1; the last three do not.

lessons.title: Two-step stories: multiply or divide first
lessons.objective: Children solve two-step story problems in which one step multiplies or divides within 100 and the other adds or subtracts.
lessons.page: Six stories ('4 bags hold 6 apples each. 5 apples are eaten. How many are left?'; '28 children sit at 4 equal tables. 2 more join one table. How many sit there now?'). Each has space for a drawing of equal groups or an array, two equation lines, and an answer line with a label. Three stories multiply first, two divide first, and in one the adding comes first. Facts within 100.

lessons.title: A letter for the unknown, and does the answer make sense?
lessons.objective: Children write one equation with a letter for the unknown for a two-step story problem, solve it, and check the answer with an estimate from rounded numbers.
lessons.page: Five two-step stories with all four operations. Each has three lines: 'My equation' (for example 3 x 8 + 19 = n), 'My estimate' (the child rounds to the nearest ten and computes), and 'My answer'. A last box asks 'Is the answer close to the estimate? yes / no'. One story at the end shows a wrong worked answer far from the estimate for the child to find and fix.

units.title: Area and Perimeter
units.why: Area is multiplication made visible, so it follows the facts and puts them to use right after winter.

lessons.title: Area of a rectangle: multiply the sides
lessons.objective: Children find the area of a rectangle from its two side lengths (whole numbers up to 10) in a story, as a product with square units.
lessons.page: Top half: six rectangles with no squares inside, labeled with two side lengths (6 ft and 4 ft); the child writes 6 x 4 = _ square feet. Bottom half: four stories with a sketch to label (a rug 8 feet long and 5 feet wide, a garden bed, a poster in inches); the child writes the equation and the answer with the square unit. Side lengths from 2 to 10; units are square inches, square feet, square centimeters and square meters.

lessons.title: Area of an L-shape
lessons.objective: Children cut an L-shaped figure into two rectangles, find the area of each by multiplying, and add the two areas.
lessons.page: Level 1: four L-shapes drawn on a grid with a dashed cut line; the child writes the product for each part and adds them. Level 2: four L-shapes on a grid with no line; the child draws the cut, and one task asks for a second way to cut. Level 3: three L-shapes with side lengths only and no grid (all sides needed are given). Side lengths from 1 to 10; areas up to 100 square units.

lessons.title: Find the missing side
lessons.objective: Children find the length of one unknown side of a polygon when the perimeter and the other side lengths are known, and write an equation with a letter for the unknown side.
lessons.page: Top half: six polygons (triangles, rectangles, a pentagon, an L-shape) with every side length written except one, which is marked with a letter, and the perimeter given ("Perimeter = 30 cm"); the child writes the equation (8 + 8 + 5 + n = 30) and the missing length. Bottom half: three stories with a sketch to label ("A garden in the shape of a rectangle has a perimeter of 26 feet. It is 9 feet long. How wide is it?"). Side lengths from 2 to 40; perimeters up to 100; units are inches, feet, centimeters and meters.

units.title: Fractions
units.why: Fractions are the newest idea of Grade 3 and get the longest unit, in late winter with time to finish before the test.

lessons.title: Unit fractions on the number line
lessons.objective: Children split the stretch from 0 to 1 on a number line into 2, 3, 4, 6 or 8 equal parts and mark and label the first part as 1/2, 1/3, 1/4, 1/6 or 1/8.
lessons.page: Top half: five number lines from 0 to 1 with the tick marks already drawn for halves, thirds, fourths, sixths and eighths; the child counts the equal parts, puts a dot at the end of the first part, and writes the unit fraction under it. Bottom half: four lines from 0 to 1 with a paper-strip picture above them and no tick marks; the child draws the ticks for the fraction asked and labels the first one. Last task: a line with unequal parts and the question 'Why is this point not 1/4?'

lessons.title: Whole numbers as fractions
lessons.objective: Children write whole numbers as fractions (3 = 3/1, 1 = 4/4, 2 = 8/4) and find the fraction and the whole number at the same point of a number line.
lessons.page: Top third: six shapes or groups of whole shapes fully shaded (one circle in fourths, two rectangles in halves); the child writes the fraction and the whole number (4/4 = 1, 4/2 = 2). Middle: three number lines from 0 to 3 marked in halves, thirds and fourths; the child writes the fraction under each whole number. Bottom: eight equations to finish (6/6 = _, 3 = _/1, 2 = _/4). Denominators 1, 2, 3, 4, 6 and 8.

units.title: Time, Mass, and Liquid Volume
units.why: Measurement in early spring gives practice in adding, subtracting and the number line with real units before the test.

units.title: Shapes and Data
units.why: Quadrilaterals, scaled graphs and line plots are the lightest unit; it starts before the test window and ends in the weeks after it.

lessons.title: Measure to the quarter inch
lessons.objective: Children measure lengths to the nearest half and quarter inch with the ruler drawn on the page and show the lengths as Xs on a line plot marked in quarters.
lessons.page: Top half: eight objects (nails, ribbons, pencils), each drawn directly above its own printed ruler marked in quarter inches, so that printing at another size changes nothing; the child writes each length (2 1/4 in., 3 1/2 in.). Bottom half: an empty line plot from 1 to 4 inches with a tick for every quarter; the child draws one X for each length and answers three questions ('How many are longer than 2 1/2 inches?'). Lengths from 1 to 4 inches.

leftOut.what: Make it balance
leftOut.why: It has no Grade 3 standard; equations with a letter are taught in the story-problem unit.

leftOut.what: Is the sum odd or even?
leftOut.why: Patterns (3.OA.D.9) keep two lessons, the pattern rule and the number machines; these two days go to two-step problems.

leftOut.what: Division with a remainder
leftOut.why: Remainders are a Grade 4 standard; Grade 3 divides within 100 with nothing left over.

leftOut.what: 12-hour and 24-hour time
leftOut.why: 24-hour time is not taught in US elementary classes and is no standard.

leftOut.what: Read a thermometer
leftOut.why: Temperature is a science topic and no Grade 3 math standard.

leftOut.what: Count the cubes
leftOut.why: Volume with cubes is a Grade 5 standard; the days go to the area of rectangles and L-shapes.

leftOut.what: A fraction of a group
leftOut.why: Grade 3 fractions are parts of one whole and points on the number line; a fraction of a set comes in Grade 4.

leftOut.what: Right angles
leftOut.why: Angles are a Grade 4 standard; the square corner is named in Is it a rectangle? with The Shape Stretcher.

leftOut.what: How many lines of symmetry?
leftOut.why: Line symmetry is a Grade 4 standard.

leftOut.what: 3.OA.C.7: one lesson for each times table
leftOut.why: Fluency is one launch lesson and the daily fact strip; table-by-table lessons would take four weeks the year does not have.

leftOut.what: 3.OA.A.3: five more story lessons (arrays and measurement stories)
leftOut.why: The existing lesson has three story pages; the new days went to two-step problems, which had nothing.

leftOut.what: 3.OA.B.5: grouping three factors, and 3.OA.B.6: a second lesson on the missing factor
leftOut.why: Breaking a fact apart is the property the class most needs; the daily strip pairs each fact with its division.

leftOut.what: 3.NBT.A.2: four more lessons (across zeros) and point 3:magic-squares
leftOut.why: Adding and subtracting within 1,000 was taught in Grade 2 and is kept up in the two-step stories; no days are left.

leftOut.what: 3.NF.A.1: two more lessons, 3.NF.A.3.a: three more, 3.NF.A.3.d: two more
leftOut.why: Fractions already have the longest unit (21 days); the two new lessons fill the standards that had no lesson at all.

leftOut.what: 3.NF.A.2.b: a new lesson
leftOut.why: The existing lesson Fractions on a number line teaches it, right after the new lesson on unit fractions.

leftOut.what: 3.MD.C.5.a and 3.MD.C.5.b: cover and count with unit squares
leftOut.why: Area: count the squares already counts unit squares with The Baking Tray; its first ten minutes cover a shape with real tiles, with no gaps and no overlaps.

leftOut.what: 3.MD.C.7.c: the area model of breaking apart
leftOut.why: The same idea is taught with arrays in Break a hard fact into two easy ones; a second page would repeat it.

leftOut.what: 3.MD.A.1, 3.MD.A.2 and 3.MD.B.3: two more lessons each, and 3.MD.D.8: same area with different perimeters
leftOut.why: No days are left; time, mass, volume and graphs keep the lessons they have today, and perimeter got the missing side.

leftOut.what: point 3:compare-4-digit
leftOut.why: Four-digit numbers are a Grade 4 standard (4.NBT.A.2).

nonTeachingWeeks.what: Routines, learning to use the math tools, and the beginning-of-year screening (counting, numerals, shapes), one child at a time.
End of the first quarter: report-card checks and family conferences.
The short week before winter break: review games and counting collections, no new lesson.
Middle-of-year benchmark window.
End of the third quarter: report-card checks and spring conferences.
End-of-year benchmark window.
Last week of school: review stations and take-home practice.

units.title: Position Words, Size, and Patterns
units.why: The year opens with words and sorting, which need no numerals and let the teacher watch every child while routines settle (weeks 3-5).

lessons.title: What can we measure?
lessons.objective: Children hold one real object (a book, a cup, a block) and say what can be measured about it: how long it is, how heavy it is, and how much it holds.
lessons.page: Circle talk with objects in hand: each pair gets one real object and tells two things about it that can be measured ('It is long. It is heavy.'); on day 2 the class checks one object on the Measurement Bench for length, weight and how much it holds. Listen for children who name a measurable attribute (long, tall, heavy, holds a lot) and not a color or a use.

units.title: Counting to 10
units.why: Counting and writing the numbers to 10 is the base of every later unit, so it comes as soon as routines are in place.

lessons.title: Touch and count
lessons.objective: Children touch and move 1 to 10 real counters one at a time into a ten-frame and say exactly one number for each counter.
lessons.page: Touch-and-count routine: each child gets a cup of 1 to 10 counters and a paper ten-frame, slides one counter into a box for each number said, and stops when the cup is empty; the teacher models on the Ten Frame tool and children count along. Listen and watch for one number word per touch: no skipped counter, no counter counted twice, no number word said without a touch.

lessons.title: Still the same number
lessons.objective: Children count 3 to 10 counters in a line, spread them out or push them together, count again, and say that the number is the same.
lessons.page: Six tasks. Each shows the same kind of object twice: once in a straight line and once spread out or in a ring (4 to 10 objects). The child counts each picture, writes the number in the box under it, and circles "same" or "not the same". In two of the six tasks the second picture really has one more or one fewer. In class children move real counters from a line into a pile and count again.

units.title: Comparing Numbers to 10
units.why: Comparing needs secure counting to 10 and comes before the class meets larger numbers.

lessons.title: Match them up: more, fewer, or the same
lessons.objective: Children pair the cubes of two groups of 1 to 10 one to one and say which group has more, which has fewer, or that the two groups are the same.
lessons.page: Six tasks, each with two rows of pictures that belong together (bees and flowers, dogs and bones), 1 to 10 in each row. The child draws a line from each picture in the top row to one in the bottom row, then circles the row with pictures left over, or colors the 'same' star when every picture has a partner. Two of the six tasks have equal groups. In class the child first pairs real cubes of two colors.

lessons.title: One more, one less
lessons.objective: Children count a group of 2 to 9 counters, put one more on or take one away, and name the new number without counting again from 1.
lessons.page: Eight tasks. Each shows a ten-frame with 2 to 9 counters and three boxes in a row marked "one less", "how many" and "one more". The child writes the number of counters in the middle box, then the numbers in the two boxes beside it. In class children build the number with real counters on a paper ten-frame, put one on or take one off, and say the new number.

lessons.title: Which number is greater?
lessons.objective: Children compare two written numbers from 1 to 10, circle the greater one, and check with two towers of real cubes.
lessons.page: A number line from 1 to 10 runs across the top. Below it are twelve pairs of written numbers from 1 to 10 in two boxes, with no pictures to count. In the first eight pairs the child circles the greater number; in the last four the child circles the number that is less. The two numbers of a pair are never the same. In class the child builds both numbers as cube towers to check.

units.title: Shapes All Around
units.why: Geometry in late fall gives number work a rest and uses the position words from the first unit.

lessons.title: Draw the shape
lessons.objective: Children build triangles, squares and rectangles with sticks and clay balls, then draw them from dot to dot and count the sides and corners.
lessons.page: Children build each shape with real sticks and clay balls first; on the dot paper they draw the named shape with straight lines from dot to dot and write how many sides and how many corners it has.

lessons.title: Flat or solid?
lessons.objective: Children sort real objects and shape cards into flat shapes and solid shapes and say how they know.
lessons.page: Children sort a basket of real things (a ball, a box, a paper circle, a paper square) into two hoops on the rug; the page shows shapes and objects, and the child marks each one as flat or solid. This teaching point is listed under Grade 2 today, and its standard is a Kindergarten standard.

lessons.title: Name the solid shapes
lessons.objective: Children roll, stack and slide real balls, cans, boxes and cones and name each one as a sphere, a cylinder, a cube or a cone, whatever its size.
lessons.page: Top half: four plain solids (sphere, cube, cylinder, cone), each with a line to draw to the everyday object of the same shape (ball, number cube, soup can, party hat). Bottom half: twelve objects and solids in different sizes, some lying on their side; the child colors them by a code of four crayons, one color for each solid name.

units.title: Counting in Order to 20
units.why: After winter break the class extends the count from 10 to 20, which the teen-numbers unit will need.

lessons.title: Write the numbers 10 to 20
lessons.objective: Children count out 10 to 20 real beans onto two ten-frames and write the number for them with both digits in the right order.
lessons.page: One row for each number from 10 to 20: a small picture of two ten-frames that shows the number, the number in gray with a start dot and arrows to trace three times, and two empty boxes to write it alone. In the last row the child writes 10 to 20 in order in eleven empty boxes. In class the child counts out that many beans before writing.

lessons.title: Count and write how many: up to 20
lessons.objective: Children count 11 to 20 real objects set out in a line, in rows or in a circle, touch each one once, and write the number.
lessons.page: The same page as Count and Write with groups of 11 to 20 pictures set out in a line, in rows of five or in a circle (never scattered); the child counts and writes the number in the box. In class children count real collections first and mark where they started.

lessons.title: Count on from a number
lessons.objective: Children start from a closed bag marked with a number from 3 to 9 and count on the 1 to 5 loose counters beside it, without starting again at 1.
lessons.page: Eight tasks. Each shows a closed bag with a number from 3 to 9 printed on it and 1 to 5 loose objects of the same kind beside it; the objects in the bag cannot be seen. The child puts a finger on the bag, says its number, counts on over the loose objects, and writes the total (4 to 14) in a box. In class children work with a real closed bag with its number written on it.

units.title: Sorting, Tallies, and the Days of the Week
units.why: Sorting and counting each kind puts the new counting to 20 to use and gives a lighter unit before addition starts.

units.title: Adding and Taking Away Within 10
units.why: Addition and subtraction begin in the second half of the year, when every child counts and writes to 10 with ease.

lessons.title: Take away: how many are left?
lessons.objective: Children put 2 to 10 counters on a ten-frame, take some away, and count how many are left.
lessons.page: Six ten-frames, each with 2 to 10 printed counters and a sentence above it ("Take away 3."). The child crosses out that many counters and completes "_ are left"; at least 1 is always left. In class children take real counters off a paper ten-frame first.

lessons.title: Some more come: adding stories
lessons.objective: Children act out stories in which some more come (totals of 3 to 10) with counters, draw them, and write the addition equation.
lessons.page: Four short stories with a small picture, read aloud by the teacher ('4 ducks swim. 2 more ducks come. How many ducks now?'). Under each story is an empty ten-frame and the frame _ + _ = _. The child draws circles for the first group, draws the ones that come in another color, and writes all three numbers. Totals from 3 to 10; no group is zero. In class children act out each story with counters first.

lessons.title: Some go away: take-away stories
lessons.objective: Children act out stories in which some go away (starting with 3 to 10) with counters, cross them out in a drawing, and write the subtraction equation.
lessons.page: Four short stories read aloud ('7 birds sit on a wire. 3 fly away. How many are still there?'). Under each story is a ten-frame that already shows the starting number as circles and the frame _ - _ = _. The child crosses out the ones that go away and writes all three numbers. Starting numbers from 3 to 10; at least 1 is left. In class children act out each story with counters first.

lessons.title: Two kinds together: put-together stories
lessons.objective: Children show stories about two kinds of things (totals of 3 to 10) with counters of two colors, color a drawing, and write the addition equation.
lessons.page: Four stories in which nothing moves ('3 red apples and 5 green apples are in the bowl. How many apples?'). Under each story is a row of ten outlined objects and the frame _ + _ = _. The child colors the two kinds in two colors, leaves the rest white, and writes all three numbers. Totals from 3 to 10; no group is zero. In class children lay out counters of two colors first.

units.title: Number Bonds and Partners of 10
units.why: Taking numbers apart follows the first adding and taking away and leads to the partners of 10, which the teen numbers build on.

lessons.title: Take apart 6 and 7
lessons.objective: Children break a train of 6 or 7 real snap cubes into two parts in different ways and write each way as an equation such as 6 = 4 + 2.
lessons.page: Top half: five uncolored cube trains of 6; bottom half: five trains of 7. The child colors each train in two colors, a different way each time, and writes the equation under it (6 = _ + _). Neither part is zero. In class children break a real cube train before they color.

lessons.title: Take apart 8 and 9
lessons.objective: Children shake and spill 8 or 9 two-color counters, sort them by color, and write the two parts in a number bond and as an equation such as 9 = 5 + 4.
lessons.page: The same page as Number Bonds Within 10 with the whole fixed at 8 (top half) and 9 (bottom half): one part is shown as dots, the child draws the dots of the other part and writes the equation 8 = _ + _. Neither part is zero. In class children shake and spill real two-color counters to find the pairs.

lessons.title: How many more to make 10?
lessons.objective: Children put 1 to 9 counters on a ten-frame and find how many more fill it to make 10.
lessons.page: Eight ten-frames, each with 1 to 9 printed counters. The child draws the missing counters in another color and writes how many were drawn in the sentence '_ more make 10'. In class children fill a paper ten-frame with real counters of a second color.

lessons.title: Partners of 10
lessons.objective: Children push some of the ten beads of a real bead string to one side and write the partner that makes 10 in an equation such as 6 + 4 = 10.
lessons.page: Nine rows. Each row shows a string of ten beads (five red, five white) with 1 to 9 beads pushed to the left, and an equation with one number missing (6 + _ = 10). The child rings the beads that are left and writes the missing number. The last three rows show the equation only. In class children slide ten beads on a string or ten cubes on a stick.

units.title: Teen Numbers and Counting to 100
units.why: Teen numbers need the full ten from the partners-of-10 lessons; the count to 100 follows in the same spring unit, near the day the daily count reaches 100, and gets the class ready for Grade 1.

lessons.title: Ten and some more
lessons.objective: Children count out 11 to 19 real straws, bundle ten of them with a rubber band, and say the number as ten and some more ones.
lessons.page: Six pictures of 11 to 19 loose objects (straws, crayons, pencils) in rows of five. The child rings ten of them, counts the ones outside the ring, and completes '10 and _' and the number. In class children bundle real straws first.

lessons.title: Teen numbers on two ten-frames
lessons.objective: Children fill one ten-frame with ten counters, put 1 to 9 more on a second frame, and write the equation, such as 13 = 10 + 3.
lessons.page: Eight tasks. Each shows two ten-frames, the first full and the second with 1 to 9 counters. The child writes the number in a box and completes the equation under it (13 = 10 + _). In class children build each number with real counters on two paper ten-frames.

lessons.title: Build and draw a teen number
lessons.objective: Children read a written number from 11 to 19, build it with ten cubes on a stick and loose cubes, and draw it on two ten-frames.
lessons.page: Six tasks. Each shows a written number from 11 to 19 and two empty ten-frames. The child draws counters to show the number (the first frame full) and completes the equation under it (15 = 10 + _). In class children build the number with a stick of ten cubes and loose cubes before they draw.

lessons.title: Ten and how many more?
lessons.objective: Children take 11 to 19 cubes apart into a stick of ten and the rest, and write the missing part in a number bond and in an equation such as 10 + 7 = 17.
lessons.page: Top half: six number bonds with a teen number as the whole and 10 as one part; the child writes the other part and completes 10 + _ = 17. Bottom half: six cards that say '10 and 4'; the child circles the right number of two (14 or 41). In class children snap ten cubes together and count the rest.

lessons.title: Count to 50
lessons.objective: Children count aloud to 50 by ones, drop one real cube into a jar for each number, and say what comes after each number that ends in nine.
lessons.page: A number chart from 1 to 50 in rows of ten with fourteen empty boxes, most of them where a new ten starts (19, 20, 21, 29, 30, 31, 39, 40, 41, 49, 50). The child says the count, touches each box, and writes the missing numbers. In class children drop a cube into a jar for each number said.

lessons.title: Count to 100 on the hundreds chart
lessons.objective: Children count aloud from 1 to 100, point to each number on a hundreds chart, and place number cards from 51 to 100 where they belong.
lessons.page: A hundreds chart with rows 1 to 50 printed in full and twenty empty boxes in rows 51 to 100, among them the last two boxes of each row. The child counts on from 50 and writes the missing numbers. In class children hang real number cards on a pocket chart.

lessons.title: Start at any number and count on
lessons.objective: Children draw a real number card from a bag (any number from 2 to 90), find it on the hundreds chart, and count on aloud from it without going back to 1.
lessons.page: Six number tracks of five boxes each. The first box holds a start number (4, 12, 28, 36, 53, 67) and the other four are empty; the child counts on and writes the next four numbers. Three of the six tracks cross into a new ten. In class children draw a number card from a bag and count on along the pocket chart.

lessons.title: Count by tens to 100
lessons.objective: Children scoop real beans into cups of ten and count the cups by tens to 100.
lessons.page: Top half: six pictures of 2 to 10 cups, each cup marked 10; the child counts by tens and circles the right number of three (30, 40 or 50). Bottom half: a path of ten stones from 10 to 100 with five numbers missing for the child to write. In class children fill real cups with ten beans each.

leftOut.what: Partners that make 20
leftOut.why: Adding in Kindergarten stays within 10; partners of 20 are Grade 1 work and take two days from the partners of 10.

leftOut.what: Odd or even?
leftOut.why: Odd and even is a Grade 2 standard (2.OA.C.3); the days go to story problems and teen numbers, which Kindergarten must teach.

leftOut.what: K.CC.A.1: a separate lesson for counting to 20
leftOut.why: The whole unit Counting in Order to 20 practices the count to 20; the three new lessons cover 50, 100 and tens.

leftOut.what: K.CC.C.6: a third lesson (count both groups to compare)
leftOut.why: The lesson More and fewer already compares by counting; matching and the equal case got the new lesson.

leftOut.what: K.OA.A.2: a fourth story lesson (choose adding or taking away)
leftOut.why: The three story types each have a lesson; mixed stories are practiced on the review day of the unit.

leftOut.what: K.OA.A.3: a fifth lesson (all the ways to make 10)
leftOut.why: The two lessons on partners of 10 teach the pairs of 10.

leftOut.what: K.OA.A.5: three more fluency lessons within 5
leftOut.why: Fluency grows from a five-minute daily practice after the strategy lessons, not from more lessons.

leftOut.what: K.NBT.A.1: a fifth teen-numbers lesson
leftOut.why: The four lessons go from objects to frames to drawings to equations; a fifth would repeat one of them.

leftOut.what: K.G.A.2: a lesson on turned shapes
leftOut.why: The lesson Name the shape already uses The Shape Stretcher to turn shapes; the new lesson went to solid shapes.
